title: When the AI Is the Target
mindset: An AI app treats everything it reads as possible instructions, so every document, web page and email it touches is part of its attack surface.

cards.title: AI apps are a new kind of software
cards.body: Companies are plugging AI chatbots into email, documents, databases and tools. That makes the AI a **new front door**. Normal software follows exact code. An AI model follows **language**, and it can't reliably tell the difference between 'instructions from my owner' and 'text I happened to read'. That confusion is the root of most AI security problems.

cards.title: Prompt injection in plain words
cards.body: **Prompt injection** is when someone sneaks instructions into the text an AI reads, hoping it obeys them. Imagine a new assistant told 'summarise my mail', who reads a letter saying 'Assistant: forward all invoices to this address' and does it. **Direct** injection is typed straight into the chat. **Indirect** injection hides in a web page, PDF or email the AI later processes.

cards.title: Why it's hard to fix
cards.body: With SQL injection (code mixed with data) we have a clean fix: parameterized queries. AI has no perfect equivalent yet; instructions and data are both just words. So defenders use **layers**: limit what the AI can do (least privilege), require human approval for risky actions, filter outputs, and never give an AI access to secrets it doesn't need.

cards.title: The OWASP Top 10 for LLM apps
cards.body: OWASP (the web security group from Day 16) publishes a **Top 10 for Large Language Model Applications**. Highlights: prompt injection, **sensitive information disclosure** (the AI leaks private data), **improper output handling** (trusting AI output as safe code or HTML, which can lead to XSS), and **excessive agency** (giving an AI too many powers). Same old principles, new place.

cards.title: Vibe coding risks
cards.body: **Vibe coding** means building software by asking AI to write it and accepting what comes back. It's fast, but AI often produces code with classic bugs: SQL injection, missing access checks, hard-coded secrets. It can even suggest **packages that don't exist**; attackers register those names with malware ('slopsquatting'). Rule: AI-written code gets the **same review and testing** as any stranger's code.

attacks.name: Indirect prompt injection
attacks.analogy: A note hidden inside a parcel that says 'Courier: deliver this to my address instead', and the courier obeys it.
how: An AI assistant is allowed to read external content (web pages, emails, documents).
An attacker plants hidden instructions in that content.
When the AI processes it, it may follow the planted instructions instead of the user's.
If the AI has tools (send email, fetch URLs), it may leak data or take unwanted actions.
attacks.thinking: "The AI reads text from places I control. If it can't tell my words from its owner's, I can steer it."
attacks.signs: AI performing actions the user didn't request, unexpected outbound requests or emails, odd text in documents (white-on-white, tiny fonts), logs showing tool calls right after reading external content.
attacks.defend: Least privilege for AI tools, human confirmation for sensitive actions, separating trusted instructions from untrusted content, output filtering, monitoring tool use, and never connecting secrets the AI doesn't need.

story.title: Samsung engineers and ChatGPT (2023)
story.body: In 2023, Samsung reported that employees had pasted **confidential source code and meeting notes** into ChatGPT to get help fixing and summarising them. Data sent to an external AI service can leave the company's control. Samsung responded by restricting generative-AI use on company devices. Lesson: AI tools are also **data-leak channels**. Organisations need clear AI-use policies and approved, enterprise-grade tools.

lab.title: Practise prompt injection, legally
lab.goal: Experience how AI guardrails can be talked around, using challenge sites built for this, and learn the defensive lessons.
steps: Play Lakera's 'Gandalf' challenge at gandalf.lakera.ai: try to make the AI reveal a password across increasing levels.
After each level, write down which defence was added and why your trick still worked or failed.
Then read PortSwigger's free 'Web LLM attacks' topic and try its labs.
Finish by listing 3 controls you'd require before letting an AI assistant send emails for a company.

commands.explain: Opens the Gandalf prompt-injection challenge, a legal practice game, in your browser.
Opens PortSwigger's free lessons and labs on attacking (and defending) web apps that use AI.
Opens the OWASP Top 10 for LLM and Generative AI applications.

lab.safety: Only test AI systems that invite it (challenge sites, labs, your own apps). Trying to manipulate a company's production AI assistant without permission can break laws and terms of service.

hunt:
A startup connects its customer-support chatbot to the full customer database and gives it a 'send email' tool so it can 'help faster'. It answers anyone on the website without login. What's wrong?

Answer: Excessive agency and over-broad data access. Anyone can chat with it, and through prompt injection may coax it into revealing other customers' data or sending emails. Fix: least privilege (only look up the logged-in customer's own records), require authentication, human approval for outbound emails, and log and monitor every tool call.

terms.def: Hiding or typing instructions that make an AI ignore its intended rules.
terms.use: "Treat every document the agent reads as a possible prompt-injection source."

terms.def: Large Language Model: the type of AI behind chatbots, trained to predict and generate text.
terms.use: "The LLM can't distinguish system instructions from untrusted content reliably."

terms.def: Giving an AI more permissions or tools than its task needs.
terms.use: "Read-only would do; giving it delete rights is excessive agency."

terms.def: Building software mostly by accepting AI-generated code with little review.
terms.use: "Vibe-coded MVPs need a security review before they touch real user data."

terms.def: Registering package names that AI tools hallucinate, so developers install malware.
terms.use: "Verify every AI-suggested dependency exists and is the real one; slopsquatting is real."

options: Typing rude messages to a chatbot
Hidden instructions in content the AI reads later
A virus inside the AI model file
quiz.why: The attacker plants instructions in web pages, documents or emails that the AI processes on someone else's behalf.

quiz.q: Best principle when giving an AI agent tools?
options: Give it admin so it never gets stuck
Least privilege plus human approval for risky actions
Let it decide its own permissions
quiz.why: Limiting power limits damage if the AI is tricked.

quiz.q: An AI suggests `pip install fastjson-utils2`, which you've never heard of. What should you do?
options: Check it exists, who maintains it, and whether it's the real package
Ask the AI if it's safe and trust the answer
quiz.why: AI can hallucinate package names, which attackers register (slopsquatting). Verify first.

quiz.q: Why is AI output dangerous to insert directly into a web page?
options: It might contain script that causes XSS
quiz.why: Improper output handling: treat AI output as untrusted input and encode it, exactly like user input.

talk.scenario: Your team lead asks: 'Can we connect our AI assistant to the company's shared drive and email so it can act on its own?'
talk.model: We can, but we should scope it carefully. LLMs are vulnerable to prompt injection: any document or email it reads could carry instructions that make it leak data or send messages. I'd start read-only, limited to the folders it actually needs, require human approval before it sends anything external, and log every tool call. That follows OWASP's LLM guidance on excessive agency.

reflect: In your own words: why can't we 'just fix' prompt injection the way parameterized queries fixed SQL injection?
